c-now-uk20.text: In 2013 the British government began to release its records when they are 20 years old instead of 30; the change was phased in between 2013 and 2022.
c-now-uk20.label: consensus

c-now-us25.text: In the United States, classified records judged to have permanent value are automatically declassified at 25 years, unless an agency obtains an approved exemption.
c-now-us25.label: consensus

c-now-leaks.text: In October 2010 Iraq Body Count reported about 15,000 'previously unknown civilian deaths contained in the Iraq War Logs released by WikiLeaks'.
c-now-leaks.label: approx
c-now-leaks.note: The figure is Iraq Body Count's own analysis of the leaked logs.

c-now-press.text: Iraq Body Count said that the deaths in the War Logs which it already had on record 'were mainly gathered from press and media reports, as well as some NGO and official figures'.
c-now-press.label: consensus

c-now-revision.text: In June 2025 the World Bank moved to new price comparisons (2021 purchasing-power parities) and revised its international poverty line from $2.15 to $3.00 a day; as a result 'the global extreme poverty rate in 2022 is revised up from 9.0 to 10.5 percent'.
c-now-revision.label: consensus

c-now-pip.text: The World Bank's live Poverty and Inequality Platform, opened on 3 November 2026, gives the world's extreme-poverty rate for 2022, at $3.00 a day, as 10.89 percent.
c-now-pip.label: approx
c-now-pip.note: A live database, revised as new surveys and prices arrive; it differs from the 10.5 percent the Bank published in June 2025.

c-now-tahtah.text: Khaled Tahtah lists problems particular to the history of the present: 'the time between an event and its documentation is short', 'the sensitivity of the issues that may be under judicial examination', and 'the issue of objectivity when interpreting events'.
c-now-tahtah.label: consensus

c-pcw-fukuyama.text: In 'The End of History?' (The National Interest, Summer 1989) Francis Fukuyama wrote of 'the universalization of Western liberal democracy as the final form of human government'.
c-pcw-fukuyama.label: consensus

c-pcw-srebrenica.text: Bosnian Serb forces under General Ratko Mladić captured Srebrenica on 11 July 1995; afterwards 'up to 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were killed or went missing'.
c-pcw-srebrenica.label: approx
c-pcw-srebrenica.note: The UN residual mechanism gives 'up to 8,000', a figure that includes the missing.

c-pcw-tribunals.text: The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ) 'both ruled that the events in Srebrenica constituted genocide'; the tribunals sentenced Ratko Mladić to life imprisonment, upheld on appeal, and in March 2019 increased Radovan Karadžić's sentence to life imprisonment on appeal.
c-pcw-tribunals.label: consensus

c-pcw-icj2007.text: In the case brought by Bosnia and Herzegovina against Serbia and Montenegro, the ICJ ruled on 26 February 2007 that Serbia 'has not committed genocide' but 'has violated the obligation to prevent genocide' in respect of the genocide at Srebrenica in July 1995, and that it had failed to co-operate fully with the ICTY by not transferring Mladić.
c-pcw-icj2007.label: consensus

c-pcw-rwanda.text: The 1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda began on 7 April and 'lasted for the 100-day period to mid-July 1994'; 'Hutu and others who opposed it were also killed'.
c-pcw-rwanda.label: consensus

c-pcw-rwanda-toll.text: Estimates of the dead in Rwanda differ: Human Rights Watch (1999) counted 'more than half a million people, three quarters of the Tutsi of Rwanda'; a Rwandan government census of 2000 listed 1,074,017 victims, 93.7 percent (1,006,354) of them Tutsi; and Luc Reydams's demographic estimate puts 'the maximum number of Tutsi genocide victims' at 'between 489,000 and 564,000'.
c-pcw-rwanda-toll.label: debated
c-pcw-rwanda-toll.note: The census's Tutsi victims alone are about twice Reydams's maximum, so the gap comes mainly from method and definition: a government list of victims against a demographic estimate of how many Tutsi lived in Rwanda and survived. Reydams also points to an undocumented census process and changed definitions of 'victim'. The census figures are as reported by Reydams (2020).

c-pcw-nato.text: NATO grew from 16 members to 32: Czechia, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999, seven states in 2004, two in 2009, one each in 2017 and 2020, Finland in 2023, and Sweden, the 32nd member, on 7 March 2024.
c-pcw-nato.label: consensus

c-pcw-eu.text: On 1 May 2004 the European Union admitted ten new members, eight of them from Central and Eastern Europe, which the EU describes as 'finally ending the division of Europe after the Second World War'; Bulgaria and Romania joined on 1 January 2007.
c-pcw-eu.label: consensus

c-pcw-mearsheimer.text: In 'Why the Ukraine Crisis Is the West's Fault' (Foreign Affairs, September/October 2014) John Mearsheimer argued that 'the United States and its European allies share most of the responsibility for the crisis' and that 'The taproot of the trouble is NATO enlargement'.
c-pcw-mearsheimer.label: debated
c-pcw-mearsheimer.note: Michael McFaul and Stephen Sestanovich replied in the same journal that Russian policy was driven by Russian politics and predated the Western mistakes. In his reply Mearsheimer wrote that 'NATO enlargement did not directly cause the crisis', calling it 'the central element of a larger strategy to move Ukraine out of Russia's orbit and integrate it into the West'.

c-pcw-critics.text: Replying in Foreign Affairs, Michael McFaul argued that Russian policy 'changed as a result of Russian internal political dynamics', and Stephen Sestanovich that 'today's aggressive Russian policy was in place long before the mistaken Western policies'.
c-pcw-critics.label: debated
c-pcw-critics.note: Replies to Mearsheimer in Foreign Affairs, November/December 2014; for the war in Ukraine see 16.5.

c-pcw-govts.text: At the Munich Conference on Security Policy on 10 February 2007 Vladimir Putin said that NATO expansion 'represents a serious provocation that reduces the level of mutual trust'. NATO states that 'NATO enlargement is not directed against Russia' and, of a promise not to enlarge, that 'Such an agreement was never made'.
c-pcw-govts.label: debated
c-pcw-govts.note: The positions of the Russian government and of NATO; the NATO page answers Russian claims about its enlargement.

c-glob2-wto.text: The World Trade Organization was established on 1 January 1995, after the Uruguay Round of trade talks (1986-94), and replaced the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) as the main multilateral trade framework.
c-glob2-wto.label: consensus

c-glob2-china-wto.text: China became 'a full member, the WTO's 143rd, on 11 December 2001'.
c-glob2-china-wto.label: consensus

c-glob2-chinashock.text: Autor, Dorn and Hanson (2016) found that 'alongside the heralded consumer benefits of expanded trade are substantial adjustment costs and distributional consequences': in the United States, where industries were exposed to Chinese imports, 'Adjustment in local labor markets is remarkably slow', with unemployment 'remaining elevated for at least a full decade', and, at the national level, 'offsetting employment gains in other industries have yet to materialize'.
c-glob2-chinashock.label: debated
c-glob2-chinashock.note: One research team's findings for the United States, in a working paper; the authors set these costs beside the gains to consumers. This page cites no rival estimate of their size.

c-glob2-poverty.text: Since June 2025 the World Bank's international poverty line has been $3.00 a day in 2021 prices (PPP), replacing $2.15 in 2017 prices; it is the median of the national poverty lines of 23 low-income countries. On this line 'about 838 million people lived in extreme poverty' in 2022, and an estimated 1.5 billion people escaped extreme poverty between 1990 and 2022.
c-glob2-poverty.label: approx
c-glob2-poverty.note: World Bank estimates, dated June 2025; under the old line the Bank had put the number escaping since 1990 at 1.3 billion.

c-glob2-owid.text: Our World in Data (August 2025) gives 817 million people in extreme poverty in 2024 under the $3 line, and says that over a generation the share fell 'from one in every two or three people to one in ten'.
c-glob2-owid.label: approx
c-glob2-owid.note: Based on World Bank data; the 2024 figure is an estimate.

c-glob2-africa.text: Under the new line, the World Bank's extreme poverty rate for Sub-Saharan Africa in 2022 rose from 37.0 to 45.5 percent.
c-glob2-africa.label: approx
c-glob2-africa.note: A revision caused by the new line and prices (June 2025), not a change on the ground.

c-glob2-pip.text: In the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform, opened on 3 November 2026, the share of the world's people below $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) is 43.41 percent in 1990 (2.30 billion people), 36.2 percent in 2000 (2.23 billion), 20.98 percent in 2010 (1.47 billion), 10.76 percent in 2019 (0.84 billion, a projection), 11.41 percent in 2020 (0.90 billion), 10.89 percent in 2022 (0.87 billion) and 10.2 percent in 2025 (0.84 billion, a nowcast).
c-glob2-pip.label: approx
c-glob2-pip.note: A live database, revised as new surveys and prices arrive; the 2019 figure is a projection and 2025 a nowcast.

c-glob2-elephant.text: Lakner and Milanovic's 'elephant curve' (1988-2008) found that the 'winners' were country-deciles that in 1988 stood around the median of the global income distribution, 90 percent of them by population in Asia, and the 'losers' those 'around the 85th percentile', almost 90 percent of them in mature economies.
c-glob2-elephant.label: debated
c-glob2-elephant.note: Influential and contested: Adam Corlett questioned how to read it, and the authors replied (see the next claims).

c-glob2-corlett.text: Adam Corlett (2016) argued that 'population growth across this period was higher in poorer countries', that the 2008 list of countries is not the same as the 1988 list, and that the weak growth in mature economies 'is actually driven by Japan and ex-Soviet satellite / Baltic states'.
c-glob2-corlett.label: debated
c-glob2-corlett.note: A critique of how the curve is read, not of whether its data are real.

c-glob2-rebuttal.text: Lakner and Milanovic replied (October 2016) that 'the non-anonymous growth incidence curve, which addresses Corlett's compositional and demographic points', was already in their original paper.
c-glob2-rebuttal.label: debated

c-glob2-gdp.text: China's National Bureau of Statistics reported that GDP 'grew 5 percent year on year in 2025', to 140.19 trillion yuan, about 20.01 trillion US dollars.
c-glob2-gdp.label: approx

c-glob2-pop.text: China's population fell for a fourth consecutive year in 2025, 'dropping by 3.39 million to 1.405 billion', and births 'dropped to 7.92 million'.
c-glob2-pop.label: approx
c-glob2-pop.note: Official figures of the National Bureau of Statistics, reported on 19 January 2026.

c-glob2-imf.text: In October 2026 the IMF cut its forecast for China's growth in 2026 to 4.5 percent and projected 4 percent for 2027, citing higher energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict, weak domestic demand and a prolonged property-sector crisis, while exports and high-tech sectors such as AI and electric vehicles grew strongly; 'Higher global oil prices, together with protracted uncertainty and structural headwinds, are expected to weigh on activity.'
c-glob2-imf.label: approx
c-glob2-imf.note: Forecasts, as reported by AFP on 14 October 2026.

c-war-911.text: On 11 September 2001 'Nineteen terrorists from al-Qaeda hijacked four commercial airplanes'; the attacks 'killed 2,977 people from 90 nations'.
c-war-911.label: consensus

c-war-afghan.text: The US air campaign in Afghanistan 'began on October 7, 2001', after the Taliban refused to hand over al-Qaeda's leaders.
c-war-afghan.label: consensus

c-war-kabul.text: In February 2020 the United States agreed with the Taliban to withdraw its troops; 'On August 15, 2021, Taliban fighters entered Afghanistan's capital, Kabul', and President Ghani fled.
c-war-kabul.label: consensus

c-war-iraq.text: US-led forces invaded Iraq on 20 March 2003 and Baghdad fell on 9 April; the war was justified by Iraq's 'alleged continued possession and manufacture of weapons of mass destruction', a claim that, in Britannica's words, 'was later proved erroneous'.
c-war-iraq.label: consensus

c-war-duelfer.text: The Iraq Survey Group's report (the Duelfer report, autumn 2004) found that Iraq had no stocks of weapons of mass destruction, its head, Charles Duelfer, testifying in October 2004 that the 'stocks do not exist', but that Saddam Hussein intended 'to resume a [chemical weapons] effort when sanctions were lifted'.
c-war-duelfer.label: consensus

c-war-ssci.text: On 5 June 2008 the Senate Intelligence Committee's chairman, Jay Rockefeller, and 'a bipartisan majority of the Committee (10-5)' released its final reports on prewar intelligence, and Rockefeller said the committee had concluded that 'the Administration made significant claims that were not supported by the intelligence'; the AP reported that the same report found the intelligence 'supported most of the administration's statements about Iraq', while officials often left out dissent and uncertainty, and the ranking Republican, Senator Kit Bond, said: 'It is ironic that the Democrats would knowingly distort and misrepresent the committee's findings.'
c-war-ssci.label: debated
c-war-ssci.note: Chairman Jay Rockefeller and the majority, including two Republicans (Chuck Hagel and Olympia Snowe), held that officials overstated the case; the committee's five other Republicans called the report partisan.

c-war-ibc.text: Iraq Body Count's database, opened on 3 November 2026, gives '200,065 - 226,628' documented civilian deaths from violence in Iraq, in monthly records running from January 2003 to February 2026.
c-war-ibc.label: approx
c-war-ibc.note: A count of documented civilian deaths only, mainly from press and media reports; deaths that were never reported are missed, as the War Logs showed.

c-war-ifhs.text: The Iraq Family Health Survey, conducted by the Iraqi government and the WHO in 9,345 households and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in January 2008, estimated that '151 000 Iraqis died from violence between March 2003 and June 2006', with a range of 104,000 to 223,000. WHO's representative in Iraq said the estimate was 'about four times lower than a smaller-scale household survey conducted earlier in 2006'.
c-war-ifhs.label: approx
c-war-ifhs.note: A household survey of violent deaths only, with a stated uncertainty range.

c-war-lancet.text: A household survey by Gilbert Burnham and colleagues (Johns Hopkins and Al Mustansiriya University, The Lancet, October 2006), in 47 clusters across Iraq, estimated that 'an additional 654 965 (ranging from 392 979 – 942 636) Iraqis have died above what would have been expected' since hostilities began in March 2003, in the period to July 2006, 91.8 percent of the additional deaths being from violence.
c-war-lancet.label: approx
c-war-lancet.note: An estimate of excess deaths from all causes, with a wide uncertainty range.

c-war-plos.text: A survey of 2,000 randomly selected households, with adults also reporting on their siblings (Hagopian and others, PLOS Medicine, 2013), estimated 'approximately 405,000 (95% uncertainty interval 48,000-751,000) excess deaths attributable to the conflict' from March 2003 to June 2011, 'more than 60%' of them directly from violence.
c-war-plos.label: approx
c-war-plos.note: A wide uncertainty interval; the authors add about 55,800 deaths in households that had emigrated.

c-war-cow.text: Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that 'over 940,000 people were killed by direct post-9/11 war violence' in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen and Pakistan in 2001-2023, 'more than 432,000' of them civilians, and that '3.6-3.8 million people died indirectly in post-9/11 war zones'.
c-war-cow.label: approx
c-war-cow.note: 'Over' marks a minimum; the indirect deaths are a range, not a count.

c-war-arabspring.text: The Arab Spring was a 'wave of pro-democracy protests and uprisings that took place in the Middle East and North Africa beginning in 2010 and 2011'; in January and February 2011 protests in Tunisia and Egypt toppled two regimes, the Tunisian uprising lasting from 17 December 2010 to 14 January 2011.
c-war-arabspring.label: consensus

c-war-syria-toll.text: The UN human rights office estimated that 'Between 1 March 2011 and 31 March 2021, 306,887 civilians were killed in the on-going war in Syria', '1.5 per cent of the total population': 143,350 deaths documented in detail and 163,537 more estimated by statistical methods.
c-war-syria-toll.label: approx
c-war-syria-toll.note: Civilians only; about half the total comes from statistical estimation ('imputation' and 'multiple systems estimation').

c-war-isis.text: ISIS took Mosul and declared a caliphate in June 2014 and at its height controlled 'over 41,000 square miles'; Mosul was retaken on 9 July 2017 and Raqqa in October 2017.
c-war-isis.label: consensus

c-war-baghuz.text: On 23 March 2019 the US-backed Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) declared at Baghuz the 'total elimination of (the) so-called caliphate'.
c-war-baghuz.label: consensus

c-war-assad.text: On 8 December 2024 rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) took Damascus, 'sending President Bashar al-Assad fleeing' and ending 'more than five decades of rule by the Assad family'.
c-war-assad.label: consensus

c-war-alawite.text: In March 2025, attacks on security forces in Syria's coastal region by forces aligned with the former government were followed by mass killings of Alawites. A government committee reported in July 'the names of 1,426 dead, including 90 women, with most of the rest being civilians', and that '238 members of the army and security forces were killed in the attacks', and said commanders 'did not give orders to commit violations'; a Reuters investigation had identified 1,479 Alawites killed; the Supreme Alawite Council rejected the findings, blamed the government of President Ahmed al-Sharaa and called for an independent UN-supervised inquiry.
c-war-alawite.label: debated
c-war-alawite.note: The government committee, Reuters' own count and the Supreme Alawite Council disagree over numbers and over responsibility.

c-war-sdf.text: After weeks of fighting in January 2026 in which government forces retook parts of northern and eastern Syria, the Kurdish-led SDF agreed on 30 January 2026 to a ceasefire and to gradual integration into the Syrian army: 'Autonomous administration institutions will be integrated into Syrian state institutions.'
c-war-sdf.label: consensus

c-war-sdf2.text: On 25 August 2026, at the presidential palace in Damascus, the SDF's commander, Mazloum Abdi, announced the group's dissolution: the SDF had completed its merger with the Syrian military and would stop operating as an independent force.
c-war-sdf2.label: consensus

c-war-syria-now.text: As the UN reported in October 2026, '5.5 million Syrians remain displaced, around 800,000 of them in camps', 'Israeli forces have held expanded territory in southern Syria since December 2024', 'sectarian tensions persist in Sweida', and the UN and Damascus have begun discussing preparations for elections.
c-war-syria-now.label: consensus

c-war-scr.text: In December 2025 the UN Security Council delisted Sharaa, Interior Minister Anas Khattab and HTS from its ISIL and Al-Qaida sanctions list; in October 2026 ISIL 'continues to pose a threat to Syrian security'.
c-war-scr.label: consensus

c-fin-fcic.text: In the crisis of 2008 millions of Americans lost their jobs, their savings and their homes. The US Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission (2011) concluded that 'this crisis was avoidable' and blamed 'widespread failures in financial regulation' and 'excessive borrowing and risk-taking by households and Wall Street'. Two dissents were filed. Keith Hennessey, Douglas Holtz-Eakin and Bill Thomas wrote that 'The financial and economic crisis began with a credit bubble in the United States and Europe' and that the majority's conclusion 'largely ignores the global nature of the crisis'; Peter J. Wallison wrote: 'I believe that the sine qua non of the financial crisis was U.S. government housing policy'.
c-fin-fcic.label: debated
c-fin-fcic.note: The commission's majority view, with the two dissents' main arguments; Wallison's dissent is quoted as reported by HousingWire.

c-fin-gse.text: The commission's majority judged that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac 'contributed to the crisis, but were not a primary cause', and that the Community Reinvestment Act 'was not a significant factor in subprime lending or the crisis'.
c-fin-gse.label: debated
c-fin-gse.note: The majority's judgment; the dissenters named in the claim above did not sign the majority report.

c-fin-miansufi.text: Atif Mian and Amir Sufi (House of Debt, 2014) argue that the Great Recession, like the Great Depression and Europe's slump, was driven by 'a large run-up in household debt followed by a significantly large drop in household spending', and that policy 'is biased toward protecting banks and creditors'.
c-fin-miansufi.label: debated
c-fin-miansufi.note: One of several explanations: Mian and Sufi put household debt at the centre, while the FCIC majority stressed failures of regulation and excessive risk-taking.

c-fin-greece.text: On 2 May 2010 the euro-area states and the IMF announced a three-year, €110 billion package for Greece: €80 billion in bilateral loans from euro-area countries and €30 billion from the IMF. Greece was to raise revenue, including by raising value-added tax, and to cut its budget deficit from 13.6 percent of GDP in 2009 to below 3 percent by 2014.
c-fin-greece.label: consensus

c-fin-spain-bubble.text: In Spain easy bank loans fed a housing bubble: house prices nearly tripled between 1997 and 2008.
c-fin-spain-bubble.label: consensus

c-fin-spain-banks.text: Spain requested a programme for its banks on 25 June 2012. The Eurogroup granted it up to €100 billion; Spain used only around €41 billion, and it exited the programme in December 2013.
c-fin-spain-banks.label: consensus

c-fin-spain-unemp.text: Spain's unemployment peaked in 2013 at an annual average of 26.2 percent, or six million unemployed. In the first quarter of 2013 the rate reached 27.16 percent (about 6.2 million people), and youth unemployment stood at 57 percent.
c-fin-spain-unemp.label: approx
c-fin-spain-unemp.note: The quarterly figure (from INE, Spain's statistics institute, via MercoPress) is higher than the annual average given by the ESM.

c-fin-esm.text: The ESM, whose first programme was Spain's bank rescue, says that after Spain exited in December 2013 'the reforms undertaken helped spark a surge in economic growth'.
c-fin-esm.label: debated
c-fin-esm.note: The judgment of the institution that ran the programme; Blanchard and Leigh (2013) found that stronger planned budget tightening had gone with lower growth than forecast, especially early in the crisis.

c-fin-multipliers.text: In January 2013 the IMF economists Olivier Blanchard and Daniel Leigh found that in advanced economies stronger planned fiscal consolidation had gone with lower growth than forecast, above all early in the crisis; their 'natural interpretation' was that 'fiscal multipliers were substantially higher than implicitly assumed by forecasters'. The relation was weaker in later years.
c-fin-multipliers.label: debated
c-fin-multipliers.note: An influential finding in the austerity debate. The authors themselves attribute the weaker relation in later years partly to forecasters learning and partly to smaller multipliers.

c-fin-brexit.text: On 23 June 2016 the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union by 51.9 to 48.1 percent (17,410,742 votes to 16,141,241) on a turnout of 72.2 percent. Scotland, where Remain won every local authority, and Northern Ireland (55.77 percent Remain) voted to stay; David Cameron resigned as prime minister.
c-fin-brexit.label: consensus

c-fin-norris.text: Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart (Cultural Backlash, 2019) explain authoritarian populism, 'as exemplified by Donald Trump in the U.S. and Brexit in the UK', by 'polarization over the cultural cleavage dividing social liberals and social conservatives'.
c-fin-norris.label: debated
c-fin-norris.note: The cultural explanation. Dani Rodrik puts the weight on economic shocks, which he sees working through culture and identity.

c-fin-rodrik.text: Dani Rodrik (2020) finds 'compelling evidence that globalization shocks, often working through culture and identity' have helped drive support for populist movements, 'particularly of the right-wing kind'; in the 2016 US presidential election, globalization-related attitudes were important correlates of the switch to Trump.
c-fin-rodrik.label: debated
c-fin-rodrik.note: Rodrik treats economic and cultural causes as interacting; Norris and Inglehart start from a cleavage over cultural values.

c-rus-georgia.text: In August 2008 Georgia and Russia fought a five-day war. A report commissioned by the European Union and led by the Swiss diplomat Heidi Tagliavini (2009) found that 'it was Georgia which triggered off the war when it attacked Tskhinvali', but that 'much of the Russian military action went far beyond the reasonable limits of defense'. Russia recognises South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent states.
c-rus-georgia.label: debated
c-rus-georgia.note: Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili said Georgia was responding to an invasion by Russian forces; the report found no evidence of this.

c-rus-crimea.text: On 27 March 2014 the UN General Assembly, by 100 votes to 11 with 58 abstentions, declared that the referendum in Crimea, 'having no validity', could not change Crimea's status. Many states said they would recognise neither the referendum nor 'the Russian Federation's subsequent illegal annexation of Crimea'.
c-rus-crimea.label: consensus

c-rus-invasion.text: Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022. On 2 March the UN General Assembly demanded that Russia 'immediately' withdraw, by 141 votes to 5 (Russia, Belarus, Eritrea, North Korea and Syria), with 35 abstentions, among them China, India and Pakistan.
c-rus-invasion.label: consensus

c-rus-civilians.text: As of January 2026 the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine had verified almost 15,000 civilian deaths; in 2025 alone at least 2,514 civilians were killed and 12,142 injured. The mission says the actual extent of civilian harm 'is likely considerably higher'.
c-rus-civilians.label: approx
c-rus-civilians.note: Verified minimum counts; the mission itself says the true toll is higher.

c-rus-military.text: Neither Moscow nor Kyiv gives timely data on military losses. In January 2026 the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated that between February 2022 and December 2025 Russia suffered 1.2 million casualties, including up to 325,000 troop deaths, and Ukraine 500,000 to 600,000 military casualties, including up to 140,000 deaths. It drew on its own analysis, interviews with officials, Mediazona and BBC data and British government estimates.
c-rus-military.label: approx
c-rus-military.note: Estimates, not counts. The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the study could not be considered 'reliable information' and that only Russia's defence ministry was authorised to give figures on losses.

c-rus-talks.text: US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine, last held in February 2026, had stalled. On 23 October Russia, Ukraine and the United States planned a trilateral round 'for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi', and on 3 November the Kremlin confirmed talks in 'Abu Dhabi from November 10-11'. Putin says the talks should deal with the security arrangements of a final peace deal, not a 'short' truce; Kyiv says it is ready to resume direct talks mediated by Washington, and Zelensky wants them 'as soon as possible'.
c-rus-talks.label: approx
c-rus-talks.note: Status as of 3 November 2026: the Abu Dhabi round had not yet taken place.

c-rus-oleshky.text: On 23 October 2026 the White House announced a local ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky, in Ukraine's Kherson region, 'to allow for humanitarian aid and the evacuation of civilians'. The pause began on Tuesday 27 October and 'ended on Sunday', 1 November, after which Russia resumed attacks; 'The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected calls for a wider ceasefire.'
c-rus-oleshky.label: approx
c-rus-oleshky.note: A local pause, not a general ceasefire. As of 2 November 2026 no general ceasefire was in force.

c-rus-uschina.text: At Busan, South Korea, on 30 October 2025 Donald Trump and Xi Jinping agreed arrangements for one year: the US halved its 20 percent fentanyl-related tariff, bringing its tariff rate on Chinese goods from 57 to 47 percent, and China agreed to delay export restrictions on five rare earth metals. Trump said Chinese purchases of US soybeans would resume immediately.
c-rus-uschina.label: approx
c-rus-uschina.note: The terms as agreed in October 2025, for one year. On 23 September 2026 the two sides agreed to extend them to 10 January 2027.

c-rus-uschina2.text: On 20 February 2026 the US Supreme Court held that 'IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs', a ruling that covered the fentanyl-related tariffs imposed on China under that law. Xi Jinping hosted Trump in Beijing in May 2026. When Xi arrived in Washington on 23 September 2026, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: 'We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan Agreement', moving its expiry from 10 November 2026 to 10 January 2027.
c-rus-uschina2.label: approx
c-rus-uschina2.note: As of 23 September 2026, as reported by Al Jazeera citing Bessent; the holding as the Court's syllabus states it, and its scope as summarised by the law firm Steptoe.

c-ip-oslo.text: On 13 September 1993 Israel and the PLO signed the Oslo accords in Washington: the PLO recognised the existence of the State of Israel, Israel recognised the PLO as the legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, and a permanent peace settlement was to be negotiated during a five-year interim period.
c-ip-oslo.label: consensus

c-ip-rabin.text: Yitzhak Rabin, Israel's prime minister, shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize with Shimon Peres and Yasser Arafat. On 4 November 1995, at the end of a peace rally in Tel Aviv, he was assassinated by a Jewish extremist.
c-ip-rabin.label: consensus

c-ip-intifada.text: Beginning in late 2000 a breakdown in negotiations between the Palestinian Authority and Israel was followed by the second, or al-Aqsa, intifada. Israel completed its pullout from Gaza in September 2005. Hamas won the Palestinian parliamentary elections of 2006 and took control of the Gaza Strip in June 2007; from September 2007 Israel imposed sanctions on the territory.
c-ip-intifada.label: consensus

c-ip-oct7.text: On 7 October 2023 Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing nearly 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and taking 251 hostages.
c-ip-oct7.label: approx
c-ip-oct7.note: Euronews gives 'nearly 1,200' and AP 1,200; the ICJ's order of January 2024 gave more than 1,200 killed and about 240 abducted, an earlier figure for the hostages.

c-ip-icj.text: On 26 January 2024, in South Africa's case against Israel under the Genocide Convention, the International Court of Justice found that 'at least some of the rights claimed by South Africa and for which it is seeking protection are plausible'. By 15 votes to 2 it ordered Israel to take steps to prevent acts covered by the Convention; by 16 votes to 1 it also ordered Israel to enable humanitarian aid, and called for the hostages' immediate and unconditional release. It did not order a ceasefire.
c-ip-icj.label: debated
c-ip-icj.note: Provisional measures, not a ruling on whether genocide occurred: as Judge Bhandari wrote, 'the Court is not deciding South Africa's claims'. Judge Sebutinde and Judge ad hoc Barak voted against the first measure. Israel's Foreign Ministry called the accusation 'wholly unfounded'.

c-ip-icj-later.text: On 24 May 2024 the ICJ ordered Israel, by 13 votes to 2, to 'Immediately halt its military offensive, and any other action in the Rafah Governorate, which may inflict on the Palestinian group in Gaza conditions of life that could bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part'. Israel's national security adviser said Israel 'has not and will not carry out' such operations. According to South Africa's presidency, Israel objected to the court's jurisdiction in its Counter-Memorial, submitted in March 2026; by an order of 21 May 2026 the court fixed 22 November 2027 for South Africa's Reply and 22 May 2029 for Israel's Rejoinder.
c-ip-icj-later.label: consensus

c-ip-ceasefire.text: A ceasefire under Donald Trump's 20-point plan took effect on 10 or 11 October 2025. On 13 October Hamas freed the last living Israeli hostages and Israel released nearly 2,000 Palestinian prisoners and detainees; the bodies of dead hostages were to be returned.
c-ip-ceasefire.label: approx
c-ip-ceasefire.note: The sources differ by a day: The Week says the fighting stopped on 10 October, the Times of Israel that the ceasefire took effect on 11 October.

c-ip-toll.text: As of 11 October 2026 Gaza's Health Ministry reported 74,377 people killed since the war began, 1,488 of them since the ceasefire (in June 2026 AP reported that the toll had surpassed 73,000). Its toll 'does not differentiate between combatants and civilians'. AP says the ministry's records are 'viewed as generally reliable by the international community'; Israel has questioned them, citing Hamas's control of the ministry. The IDF says it has killed over 24,000 combatants in Gaza.
c-ip-toll.label: debated
c-ip-toll.note: The ministry is part of Gaza's Hamas-run administration; AP reports its records are generally accepted internationally, while Israel disputes them. The IDF's figure for combatants is its own claim.

c-ip-lancet.text: A peer-reviewed household survey led by Michael Spagat (The Lancet Global Health, February 2026), with fieldwork by Khalil Shikaki's Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, estimated 75,200 violent deaths in the war's first 15 months, 'a figure far higher than the 49,000 deaths local health officials announced at the time', and about 16,300 non-violent deaths. Women, children and the elderly made up 56.2 percent of the violent deaths.
c-ip-lancet.label: approx
c-ip-lancet.note: A survey estimate, so subject to sampling uncertainty; it covers only the first 15 months.

c-ip-idf71.text: In January 2026 a senior Israeli military official, speaking anonymously, put the death toll in Gaza at about 71,000; the IDF said the details published 'do not reflect official IDF data'.
c-ip-idf71.label: debated
c-ip-idf71.note: An unofficial estimate that the IDF disowned as official data; it was close to the ministry's figure at the time.

c-ip-phase2.text: A year after the ceasefire of October 2025 the second phase of Trump's plan, under which Hamas was to disarm, had stalled. At the end of July 2026 Trump announced an agreement for the 'COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas', to be 'carried out in carefully structured phases', and the Board of Peace issued a joint statement with the mediators; Hamas said it had agreed to a deal 'aimed at fully ending Israel's war on Gaza', but that laying down its heavy weapons 'was contingent on the creation of a Palestinian state', and an Israeli official said 'there will be no Israeli withdrawal before the militant group is disarmed and the strip demilitarized'. As of 10 October 2026 'disarmament has yet to take place', 'Israeli forces now control about 70 percent of Gaza', against about 53 percent under the ceasefire's initial terms, 'Israel has refused to reciprocate by starting to withdraw forces', and, according to Hürriyet Daily News, 'Most of Gaza's population remains displaced'.
c-ip-phase2.label: debated
c-ip-phase2.note: Status as of 10 October 2026. Hamas ties disarmament to Israeli withdrawal and to Palestinian statehood; Israel requires disarmament before any withdrawal. The figures for June 2026 (about 60 percent of Gaza held, 1.7 million people in tents, from The Week) are superseded.

c-ip-recognition.text: On 21 September 2025 the UK, Australia and Canada formally recognised a Palestinian state; Keir Starmer said they joined 'over 150 countries'. Mahmoud Abbas called the moves 'an important and necessary step toward achieving a just peace in accordance with international law'. Benjamin Netanyahu said a Palestinian state 'will not happen', and Donald Trump said he disapproved of the British move.
c-ip-recognition.label: consensus

c-latsp-argentina.text: In December 2001 Argentina defaulted on its sovereign debt and soon afterwards abandoned the convertibility regime, under which the peso had been pegged at parity with the US dollar since 1991; the crisis had 'a devastating economic and social impact'. In 2004 the IMF's Independent Evaluation Office concluded that 'the IMF erred by supporting inadequate policies too long'.
c-latsp-argentina.label: consensus

c-latsp-milei.text: Javier Milei has governed Argentina since December 2023. In the midterm elections of 26 October 2025 his party, La Libertad Avanza, won 40.84 percent of the votes cast for Congress. His reforms slowed inflation by two-thirds, alongside faltering economic growth, consumption and manufacturing; he cut tens of thousands of public sector jobs, and the US pledged a $40 billion aid package.
c-latsp-milei.label: debated
c-latsp-milei.note: The fall in inflation was a relief to many; critics blamed his reforms for 'plunging millions of Argentines deeper into poverty' in their early phase, and voters cited corruption scandals in his inner circle (RTÉ, October 2025).

c-latsp-venezuela.text: As of November 2024 the R4V platform, coordinated by the IOM and UNHCR, counted at least 7.9 million Venezuelans who had left their country, more than 6.7 million of them in the 17 countries of the R4V response.
c-latsp-venezuela.label: approx
c-latsp-venezuela.note: The count rests on host governments' records and so misses people without regular status; the source says 'La cifra con seguridad es más alta' (the figure is certainly higher). Figures for 2025-26 could not be confirmed.

c-latsp-maduro.text: On 3 January 2026 US forces seized Venezuela's leader, Nicolás Maduro, and his wife, Cilia Flores, from their home on a military base; Trump said the US turned off the lights in the capital, Caracas, while its forces moved in. They were flown to New York, where a new indictment accused them of a narco-terrorism conspiracy. Trump said: 'We're going to run the country until such time as we can do a safe, proper and judicious transition.'
c-latsp-maduro.label: debated
c-latsp-maduro.note: Legal experts immediately questioned whether the operation was lawful, and it was carried out without congressional approval. Maduro's government called it an 'imperialist attack', and Vice President Delcy Rodríguez at first declared that Maduro was still the only president.

c-latsp-rodriguez.text: By September 2026 Delcy Rodríguez was Venezuela's acting president. At the UN General Assembly on 23 September 2026 she said 'Elections will be held in Venezuela' but gave no date; unnamed critics say Washington has sidelined the Venezuelan opposition, 'dropping demands for free elections in favour of oil and investment deals with the interim government'. On 29 October she said 'Habrá elecciones' (there will be elections), to be 'organizadas por una autoridad electoral renovada' (organised by a renewed electoral authority), again without a date. The opposition, led by María Corina Machado, who returned to Venezuela on 25 October 'after almost a year in exile', and Edmundo González Urrutia, demands 'elecciones presidenciales en 2027' (presidential elections in 2027).
c-latsp-rodriguez.label: approx
c-latsp-rodriguez.note: Status as of 29 October 2026: no election date had been set. Spanish quotations from EFE, with translations.

c-latsp-mexico.text: INEGI, Mexico's autonomous statistics institute, reported in August 2026 that the homicide rate fell to 21.4 per 100,000 people in 2025 (27,989 homicides, against 33,550 in 2024), from 25.6 in 2024; its highest level was 29, in 2018, 2019 and 2020.
c-latsp-mexico.label: approx
c-latsp-mexico.note: INEGI counts from the states' death registrations; the government's own figures come from prosecutors' investigation files, so the two series differ.

c-latsp-bolsonaro.text: On 11 September 2025 a five-justice panel of Brazil's Supreme Court voted 4 to 1 to convict the former president Jair Bolsonaro of plotting a military coup to overturn the 2022 election, and sentenced him to more than 27 years in prison.
c-latsp-bolsonaro.label: debated
c-latsp-bolsonaro.note: Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing, and his lawyers called the sentence 'excessive and disproportionate' and said they would appeal; the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, called the case a 'witch hunt'.

c-latsp-eta.text: ETA, created under Franco's dictatorship to seek an independent Basque country, killed 853 people. On 20 October 2011 it declared a 'definitive end' to its terrorism; it declared itself disarmed in 2017, and on 2 May 2018 it announced that it had 'dissolved all its structures'.
c-latsp-eta.label: consensus

c-latsp-catalonia.text: On 1 October 2017 Catalonia held an independence referendum that Spain's Constitutional Court had suspended and the Spanish government had declared illegal. The Catalan government reported that 90.9 percent of those who voted backed independence, on a turnout of 42.3 percent. On 27 October the Catalan parliament declared independence; Mariano Rajoy, who had warned he would activate Article 155 of the constitution, dismissed Carles Puigdemont's government and called snap elections, and Puigdemont left for Belgium.
c-latsp-catalonia.label: debated
c-latsp-catalonia.note: The Catalan government and parliament acted on the result; the Spanish government and the Constitutional Court held the vote illegal. GlobalSecurity puts turnout at 'only 43 percent'.

c-latsp-amnesty.text: After the inconclusive 2023 elections Pedro Sánchez proposed an amnesty for those involved in the Catalan independence push, including the 2017 bid, in exchange for support in parliament from Catalan secessionist parties, which helped him stay on as prime minister; conservatives opposed it. On 16 July 2026 the EU Court of Justice ruled that 'EU law does not preclude the Spanish amnesty law', which could pave the way for the exiled Puigdemont's return.
c-latsp-amnesty.label: debated
c-latsp-amnesty.note: Sánchez's government backed the law and conservatives opposed it. The court ruled only on its compatibility with EU law.

c-pop-1991.text: In 1991, in the face of a huge balance-of-payments deficit, India's finance minister, Manmohan Singh, began reforms that opened up the economy, moving India, in the AP's words, away from 'a socialist-patterned economy' and toward 'a capitalist model'.
c-pop-1991.label: consensus

c-pop-growth.text: As of November 2025 the World Bank called India the fastest-growing major economy, with growth of 6.5 percent in 2024-25.
c-pop-growth.label: approx
c-pop-growth.note: World Bank figure for India's fiscal year 2024-25, from its country overview updated on 10 November 2025.

c-pop-newseries.text: On 27 February 2026 India's Ministry of Statistics released a new GDP series with 2022-23 as its base year, replacing 2011-12, and estimated real growth in 2025-26 at 7.6 percent. Its provisional estimate, released on 5 June 2026, put growth in 2025-26 at 7.7 percent.
c-pop-newseries.label: approx
c-pop-newseries.note: Official estimates under the new series: the advance figure as reported by PTI on 27 February 2026, and the provisional figure as reported by ThePrint on 5 June 2026.

c-pop-gdpdebate.text: In 2019 Arvind Subramanian, a former chief economic adviser to the government, argued in a paper published at Harvard that India's growth between 2011-12 and 2016-17 had been about 4.5 percent a year rather than the official 7 percent. The Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister rejected the claim, faulting his 'blind trust in a private agency (CMIE)' and his neglect of services and farm data.
c-pop-gdpdebate.label: debated
c-pop-gdpdebate.note: Subramanian gave a 95 percent confidence interval of 3.5-5.5 percent. The council's reply had as its primary contributors the economists Bibek Debroy, Rathin Roy, Surjit Bhalla, Charan Singh and Arvind Virmani.

c-pop-imf.text: In its 2025 Article IV report the IMF graded India's national accounts data 'C', the second-lowest grade on its A-D scale, for the second year running, meaning the data have shortcomings that 'somewhat hamper surveillance'. It cited the old 2011-12 base year among other problems. A statement by Indian officials, among them Urjit Patel, India's executive director at the IMF, noted that IMF staff had found the statistics 'broadly adequate for surveillance' and argued that better ratings were warranted.
c-pop-imf.label: debated
c-pop-imf.note: Reported by Business Standard on 28 November 2025. The new GDP series of February 2026 (base year 2022-23) was expected to help win a better grade.

c-pop-poverty.text: Measured at the World Bank's line of US$2.15 a day, extreme poverty in India fell from 16.2 percent in 2011-12 to 2.3 percent in 2022-23, lifting 171 million people above the line. At the newer line of US$3.00 a day (2021 prices) it fell from 27.1 percent to 5.3 percent.
c-pop-poverty.label: approx
c-pop-poverty.note: World Bank estimates. The figure depends on the poverty line chosen (on poverty lines, see 16.2).

c-pop-india-china.text: The UN projected that in April 2023 India would overtake China as the world's most populous country.
c-pop-india-china.label: approx
c-pop-india-china.note: A projection from UN population estimates, not the result of a count.

c-pop-8bn.text: The UN marked 15 November 2022 as the day the world's population reached 8 billion.
c-pop-8bn.label: approx
c-pop-8bn.note: A symbolic date: the UN said the world's population was 'projected to reach 8 billion' that day.

c-pop-peak.text: The UN's World Population Prospects 2024 projects growth from 8.2 billion people in 2024 to a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s, followed by a slight fall to about 10.2 billion by the end of the century.
c-pop-peak.label: approx
c-pop-peak.note: A projection published in July 2024; it rests on assumptions about future births and deaths.

c-pop-fertility.text: Between 1990 and 2024 world fertility fell from 3.31 children per woman to 2.25, and life expectancy at birth rose from 64.0 to 73.3 years; women are having, on average, one child fewer than around 1990.
c-pop-fertility.label: approx
c-pop-fertility.note: UN estimates (World Population Prospects 2024), as summarised by INED.

c-pop-peaked.text: Population size has already peaked in 63 countries and areas, among them China, Germany, Japan and Russia; one in four people live in such a country.
c-pop-peaked.label: approx

c-pop-africa.text: Sub-Saharan Africa's population is projected to rise by about two-thirds by 2050. In nine countries, among them Angola, the Central African Republic, DR Congo, Niger and Somalia, it is projected to double between 2024 and 2054, and Nigeria, India, Pakistan and the United States are among 126 countries expected to keep growing through 2054. China's population, by contrast, is projected to fall by about 200 million, close to 14 percent, between 2024 and 2054.
c-pop-africa.label: approx

c-pop-ageing.text: By the late 2070s people aged 65 and over are projected to outnumber children under 18.
c-pop-ageing.label: approx

c-pop-migrants.text: The UN counts 304 million international migrants in 2024, 3.7 percent of the world's population, nearly double the estimated 154 million of 1990; their share of world population has risen only modestly, from 2.9 percent in 1990.
c-pop-migrants.label: approx

c-pop-remit.text: The World Bank expected officially recorded remittances to low- and middle-income countries to reach $685 billion in 2024, with India the largest recipient at about $129 billion and Mexico second at about $68 billion.
c-pop-remit.label: approx
c-pop-remit.note: Estimates published in December 2024. The World Bank says the true total, including informal channels, is likely larger.

c-relig-christians.text: Between 2010 and 2020 the number of Christians rose by 122 million, to 2.3 billion, but their share of the world's population fell 1.8 percentage points, to 28.8 percent.
c-relig-christians.label: approx
c-relig-christians.note: Pew Research Center estimates, published June 2025.

c-relig-muslims.text: Between 2010 and 2020 the number of Muslims rose by 347 million, more than all other religions combined, and their share of the world's population rose 1.8 points, to 25.6 percent. Pew attributes the growth largely to Muslims' 'relatively young age structure and high fertility rate'.
c-relig-muslims.label: approx
c-relig-muslims.note: Pew Research Center estimates, published June 2025.

c-relig-nones.text: The religiously unaffiliated rose by 270 million, to 1.9 billion, or 24.2 percent of the world's population, and Pew finds: 'Religious disaffiliation is the main driver of the decline in the Christian share'.
c-relig-nones.label: approx
c-relig-nones.note: Pew's 2015 projections had expected the unaffiliated share to fall from 16 percent in 2010 to 13 percent by 2050; the two reports use different baselines, so projections should be read with care.

c-relig-others.text: Hindus rose by 126 million, to 1.2 billion, holding steady at 14.9 percent. Buddhists fell by 19 million, to 324 million (4.1 percent), the only major group with fewer people in 2020 than in 2010. Jews grew by nearly 1 million, to 14.8 million, and held steady as a share.
c-relig-others.label: approx

c-relig-south.text: As of 2020, 30.7 percent of the world's Christians lived in sub-Saharan Africa, compared with 22.3 percent in Europe.
c-relig-south.label: approx

c-relig-proj2015.text: Pew's projections of 2015 expected near parity by 2050 between Muslims (2.8 billion, or 30 percent of the world's population) and Christians, and that four out of every ten Christians would then live in sub-Saharan Africa.
c-relig-proj2015.label: approx
c-relig-proj2015.note: Projections made in 2015 from 2010 data; Pew's later estimates use updated baselines.

c-relig-pente.text: Pew estimated that in 2010 there were about 279 million pentecostal and 305 million charismatic Christians, together about 584 million.
c-relig-pente.label: approx
c-relig-pente.note: A 2011 estimate for 2010. The categories are defined differently by different counters, so totals vary.

c-relig-jews.text: Counts of the world's Jews depend on who is counted. Pew gives 14.8 million for 2020. The demographer Sergio DellaPergola estimated a 'core' Jewish population of 15,736,800 on 1 January 2024, 7,153,000 of them in Israel and 6.3 million in the United States; his wider 'enlarged' estimate is 21,774,677, and he puts the total Jewish and non-Jewish population eligible to immigrate to Israel under its Law of Return at about 24.7 million.
c-relig-jews.label: approx
c-relig-jews.note: DellaPergola defines the core population as those who consider Judaism 'their mutually exclusive identification framework'. The figures are for different years and definitions.

c-relig-israelpop.text: In September 2025 Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics put the country's population at 10,148,000, of whom about 7.76 million were counted as 'Jews and others' and 2.13 million as Arabs.
c-relig-israelpop.label: approx
c-relig-israelpop.note: Official estimate on the eve of Rosh Hashanah, 2025, as reported by Ynetnews.

c-relig-benedict.text: Benedict XVI resigned as from 28 February 2013, the first pope to resign since Gregory XII in 1415.
c-relig-benedict.label: consensus

c-relig-francis.text: Francis, elected on 13 March 2013, was the first Latin American leader of the Roman Catholic Church. He died of a stroke and heart failure on Easter Monday, 21 April 2025, aged 88.
c-relig-francis.label: consensus

c-relig-leo.text: On 8 May 2025 the cardinals elected Robert Prevost, who took the name Leo XIV, the first American pope. A member of the Augustinian order, he had served as a missionary in Peru, later led the church in Chiclayo, held Peruvian citizenship from 2015, and before his election headed the Vatican office that vets the appointment of bishops.
c-relig-leo.label: consensus

c-relig-leaders.text: In Pew surveys across 35 countries, published in January 2025, a median of 30 percent said it is very important that their leader stand up for people with their religious beliefs: around seven in ten in Bangladesh and Indonesia, about three in ten in the United States, Israel and Chile, 11 percent in France and 5 percent in Japan. A median of 22 percent said it is very important that the leader share their own religious beliefs, 48 percent in middle-income countries against 10 percent in high-income ones.
c-relig-leaders.label: approx
c-relig-leaders.note: Pew surveys drawing on its spring 2024 survey data.

c-clim-ipcc.text: The IPCC's Sixth Assessment (Synthesis Report, 2023) concludes: 'Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming'. It finds that global surface temperature was 1.1°C above 1850-1900 in 2011-2020.
c-clim-ipcc.label: consensus

c-clim-paths.text: In the IPCC's modelled pathways that limit warming to 1.5°C with no or limited overshoot, greenhouse-gas emissions fall by a median of 43 percent by 2030 and 60 percent by 2035, compared with 2019.
c-clim-paths.label: approx
c-clim-paths.note: Medians of many modelled pathways; the ranges are 34-60 percent for 2030 and 49-77 percent for 2035 (Table SPM.1).

c-clim-near15.text: The IPCC judged it 'more likely than not' that warming would reach 1.5°C in the near term (2021-2040), even under its very low-emission scenario.
c-clim-near15.label: approx
c-clim-near15.note: 'More likely than not' is the IPCC's calibrated term for a probability above 50 percent.

c-clim-paris.text: The Paris Agreement was adopted by 195 Parties at COP21 in Paris on 12 December 2015 and entered into force on 4 November 2016. It aims to hold warming 'well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels' and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. As of 27 January 2026 it had 194 Parties.
c-clim-paris.label: consensus

c-clim-us.text: The withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement took effect on 27 January 2026, making it the only country to quit the pact twice.
c-clim-us.label: consensus

c-clim-2024.text: The World Meteorological Organization confirmed 2024 as the warmest year on record, about 1.55°C (±0.13°C) above the pre-industrial level, but stressed that one such year 'does NOT mean that we have failed to meet Paris Agreement long-term temperature goals'.
c-clim-2024.label: approx
c-clim-2024.note: The margin of error is ±0.13°C. The Paris goals refer to long-term warming, not single years.

c-clim-2025.text: Copernicus ranked 2025 the third-warmest year on record, at 1.47°C above pre-industrial, and found that 2023-2025 was the first three-year period to average more than 1.5°C; it warned that the 1.5°C long-term limit could be reached by the end of this decade.
c-clim-2025.label: approx
c-clim-2025.note: Copernicus estimate; other datasets give slightly different figures.

c-clim-gcp.text: The Global Carbon Project projected that fossil CO2 emissions would reach a record 38.1 billion tonnes in 2025, and estimated that just 170 billion tonnes could still be emitted while keeping to 1.5°C.
c-clim-gcp.label: approx
c-clim-gcp.note: A projection for the full year 2025, made before the year ended.

c-clim-edgar.text: By the EDGAR database's count, the world emitted a record 54 billion tonnes of greenhouse gases (CO2-equivalent) in 2025, 0.7 percent more than in 2024. China emitted 15,981 million tonnes (29.5 percent of the total), the United States 6,018 million (11.1 percent), India 4,508 million (8.3 percent), the EU 3,127 million (5.8 percent) and Russia 2,574 million (4.8 percent). The US had the largest absolute rise, 2.2 percent, while China's emissions rose 0.1 percent and India's fell 0.2 percent.
c-clim-edgar.label: approx
c-clim-edgar.note: European Commission JRC estimates published September 2026, for all greenhouse gases excluding land use and forestry.

c-clim-cumul.text: Measured by cumulative CO2 since 1850, including land use and forestry, the United States had emitted more than 509 billion tonnes by the end of 2021, 20.3 percent of the world total, and China 11.4 percent. The Union of Concerned Scientists notes: 'Cumulative carbon dioxide emissions are the dominant driver of climate change.'
c-clim-cumul.label: approx
c-clim-cumul.note: Carbon Brief analysis of October 2021, for 1850-2021.

c-clim-cop30deal.text: At COP30 in Belém in November 2025 rich nations agreed to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035, but a 'roadmap' for moving away from fossil fuels, pushed by the EU and others, was dropped from the final text; Brazil's presidency issued a separate text on fossil fuels and forests outside the main accord.
c-clim-cop30deal.label: consensus

c-clim-cop30views.text: France's ecological transition minister, Monique Barbut, accused Saudi Arabia, Russia, India and 'many' other emerging countries of refusing language on phasing out fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia's deputy environment minister, Osama Faqeeha, said 'the issue is the emissions, it's not the fuel'; India said it did not oppose a plan, but that countries must not be 'called to adhere to a uniform pathway', and, speaking for a group of developing countries: 'Adaptation is a priority.'
c-clim-cop30views.label: debated
c-clim-cop30views.note: Carbon Brief found that an informal list of 84 'blocking' countries drawn up at the conference contained contradictions and likely errors.

c-clim-solar.text: IRENA puts the cost of electricity from new solar photovoltaic plants commissioned in 2024 at US$0.043 per kWh, on average 41 percent cheaper than the lowest-cost fossil-fuel alternatives, and finds that 91 percent of new renewable projects commissioned that year were more cost-effective than any new fossil-fuel alternative.
c-clim-solar.label: approx
c-clim-solar.note: IRENA figures published July 2025. IRENA itself notes that grid-connection bottlenecks delay projects and that high capital costs in many developing countries raise the cost of renewables.

c-clim-cost.text: Estimates of the costs and benefits of cutting emissions differ widely. The Stern Review (2006) found that unchecked climate change would be 'equivalent to losing at least 5 percent of global GDP each year now and forever', while action could be limited to around 1 percent of global GDP a year. Bjørn Lomborg writes of net-zero promises: 'Every dollar in cost delivers perhaps 16 cents of climate benefits.'
c-clim-cost.label: debated
c-clim-cost.note: Two positions, neither a consensus: Nicholas Stern's estimates date from 2006, Lomborg's from a December 2023 opinion column.

c-tech-internet.text: About 6 billion people, almost three-quarters of the world's population, were using the internet in 2025, according to the ITU; 2.2 billion remained offline, most of them in low- and middle-income countries.
c-tech-internet.label: approx

c-tech-haidt.text: Whether smartphones and social media caused a rise in teenage anxiety and depression is disputed. The core idea of Jonathan Haidt's The Anxious Generation (2024), in Fortune's summary, is that 'something changed in the lives of American young people somewhere around 2010 to 2015', and Zach Rausch, Haidt's chief researcher, says that much of what the book has focused on is 'irrefutable'. Candice Odgers of the University of California, Irvine, says Haidt is 'telling stories that are unsupported by research', and Andrew Przybylski of Oxford: 'Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.'
c-tech-haidt.label: debated
c-tech-haidt.note: The dispute is over causation: some critics point to studies showing 'correlation rather than causation'.

c-tech-ban.text: Australia's ban on social media accounts for children under 16 took effect on 10 December 2025; platforms that fail to take reasonable steps to remove such accounts face fines of up to A$49.5 million.
c-tech-ban.label: consensus

c-tech-bandebate.text: By mid-January 2026 ten platforms had reported revoking about 4.7 million accounts belonging to Australian children. Meta criticised the law, arguing that 'blanket bans are not the solution', as did privacy advocates and some groups representing teenagers; some young people said they had got around it, and the eSafety Commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, said there were no long-term trends yet.
c-tech-bandebate.label: debated
c-tech-bandebate.note: Whether the ban works is not yet known; the account figures were reported by the platforms and not broken down by platform.

c-tech-wuhan.text: On 31 December 2019 WHO's country office in China picked up a media statement by the Wuhan Municipal Health Commission on cases of 'viral pneumonia' in Wuhan. WHO declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern on 30 January 2020 and characterized COVID-19 as a pandemic on 11 March 2020.
c-tech-wuhan.label: consensus

c-tech-reported.text: By December 2024 more than 7 million deaths from COVID-19 had been reported to WHO, which says the true numbers are likely higher.
c-tech-reported.label: approx
c-tech-reported.note: Cumulative deaths reported to WHO, as of December 2024.

c-tech-excess.text: WHO estimates about 14.9 million excess deaths (range 13.3 to 16.6 million) associated with the pandemic in 2020 and 2021 alone. Excess mortality is 'the difference between the number of deaths that have occurred and the number that would be expected'; 81 percent of the excess deaths were in middle-income countries, and 68 percent in just ten countries.
c-tech-excess.label: approx
c-tech-excess.note: A modelled estimate published in May 2022, covering two years only, so not directly comparable with the cumulative reported total.

c-tech-excess2.text: In World Health Statistics 2026 WHO estimated global excess deaths from 2020 to 2023 at 22.1 million, 'far surpassing the 7.0 million reported COVID-19 deaths'; excess mortality 'peaked in 2021 at 10.4 million'.
c-tech-excess2.label: approx
c-tech-excess2.note: WHO's latest estimate, a modelled figure covering 2020 to 2023; it supersedes the 2020-21 estimate as WHO's most recent, though that figure remains correct for those two years.

c-tech-mrna.text: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning nucleoside base modifications that enabled effective mRNA vaccines against COVID-19. Two such vaccines, with protective effects of around 95 percent, were approved as early as December 2020, and by the time of the prize more than 13 billion COVID-19 vaccine doses had been given worldwide.
c-tech-mrna.label: consensus

c-tech-nobel24.text: John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton won the 2024 Nobel Prize in physics 'for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks'.
c-tech-nobel24.label: consensus

c-tech-aidebate.text: Some scientists, including Hinton, worry that AI could become superintelligent; many researchers disagree that it is on such a path.
c-tech-aidebate.label: debated
c-tech-aidebate.note: Science News (October 2024) reports both views without settling them.

c-tech-transformer.text: In June 2017 Google researchers proposed the Transformer, 'a new simple network architecture' based 'solely on attention mechanisms', in the paper 'Attention Is All You Need'.
c-tech-transformer.label: consensus

c-tech-chatgpt.text: OpenAI launched ChatGPT on 30 November 2022. Britannica describes it as one of several large language models, based on the 'Generative Pre-training Transformer' architecture, that can sometimes produce inaccurate information.
c-tech-chatgpt.label: consensus

c-tech-users.text: On 27 February 2026 OpenAI announced that ChatGPT had reached 900 million weekly active users.
c-tech-users.label: approx
c-tech-users.note: The company's own figure, reported by TechCrunch.

c-tech-present.text: The historian Timothy Garton Ash describes the history of the present as 'this strange mongrel genre', written 'between journalism and scholarship'.
c-tech-present.label: consensus

pages.title: The present age
pages.lede: This chapter runs from 1991 to November 2026, a stretch of history whose records are still opening. Britain releases most government files only after 20 years and the United States declassifies classified records automatically only after 25, so historians lean on journalism, leaked documents and statistics that are themselves revised, and their judgments about the very recent past are provisional.
body: The chapter follows on from the end of the Cold War (15.14). Its first pages take up genocide in Rwanda in 1994 [[c-pcw-rwanda]] and at Srebrenica in 1995 (16.1), [[c-pcw-srebrenica]] the World Trade Organization, which China joined in 2001 (16.2), [[c-glob2-china-wto]] and the attacks of 11 September 2001 and the wars that followed, down to the fall of Bashar al-Assad in Syria in December 2024 (16.3). [[c-war-911]] [[c-war-assad]] Later pages turn to the financial crisis, Russia and Ukraine, Israel and the Palestinians, Latin America and Spain, population, religion, climate, and technology and health (16.4 to 16.11).

Many official records of these years are still closed. In 2013 the British government began to release its records at 20 years old instead of 30, a change phased in by 2022. [[c-now-uk20]] In the United States, classified records judged to have permanent value are declassified automatically at 25 years, unless an agency obtains an exemption, [[c-now-us25]] so American classified records from 2003, the year of the invasion of Iraq, reach that age only in 2028.

Journalism and leaks fill part of the gap. Iraq Body Count said the deaths in its records that also appeared in the leaked Iraq War Logs 'were mainly gathered from press and media reports, as well as some NGO and official figures'. [[c-now-press]] The logs themselves, released by WikiLeaks in October 2010, held about 15,000 civilian deaths that Iraq Body Count had not known of. [[c-now-leaks]]

Even statistics move. In June 2025 the World Bank adopted new price comparisons and raised its poverty line from $2.15 to $3.00 a day, and its estimate of the share of the world's people in extreme poverty in 2022 went up from 9.0 to 10.5 percent. [[c-now-revision]] Its live database, opened for this page on 3 November 2026, gives 10.89 percent for the same year. [[c-now-pip]] The historian Khaled Tahtah adds that in the history of the present 'the time between an event and its documentation is short', some of its subjects may still be before the courts, and there is 'the issue of objectivity when interpreting events'. [[c-now-tahtah]] For these reasons this chapter dates every figure and names the body behind it.

practice.q: Why should a historian writing in 2026 treat accounts of the American decision to invade Iraq in 2003 as provisional?
choices: Classified US records from 2003 are not yet due for release
Journalism can no longer serve as a source for recent wars
Leaked documents have added little to the documented record
Britain released its records on the war in full in 2013
practice.why: Under the 25-year rule, classified US records from 2003 reach that age only in 2028, and agencies can obtain exemptions.

wrong.1: Iraq Body Count's records were mainly gathered from press and media reports.
wrong.2: The Iraq War Logs of 2010 held about 15,000 civilian deaths that Iraq Body Count had not known of.
wrong.3: 2013 is when Britain began moving to release records at 20 years old instead of 30, a change phased in up to 2022.

practice.q: The World Bank's estimate of extreme poverty in 2022 rose from 9.0 to 10.5 percent in June 2025. What explains the change?
choices: The Bank adopted new prices and a higher line of $3.00 a day
Poverty rose sharply on the ground between 2022 and 2025
The Bank lowered its poverty line from $3.00 to $2.15
New surveys found more poor people in Sub-Saharan Africa
practice.why: The Bank moved to 2021 purchasing-power parities and raised its line from $2.15 to $3.00 a day. When the definition changes, the count changes, even for a past year.

wrong.1: The revision changed the estimate for 2022 itself; it came from a new line and new prices, not from later events.

pages.title: After the Cold War
pages.lede: In 1989 Francis Fukuyama wrote of Western liberal democracy becoming universal. The decade that followed brought genocide in Rwanda in 1994 and at Srebrenica in 1995, while NATO and the European Union took in states of Central and Eastern Europe, an enlargement whose part in Russia's later hostility is still disputed.
body: In an essay titled 'The End of History?', published in the summer of 1989, Francis Fukuyama wrote of 'the universalization of Western liberal democracy as the final form of human government'. [[c-pcw-fukuyama]] The events on this page, and in the rest of the chapter, are one test of that claim.

On 11 July 1995 Bosnian Serb forces under General Ratko Mladić captured the town of Srebrenica, and afterwards up to 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were killed or went missing. [[c-pcw-srebrenica]] Both the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the International Court of Justice ruled that the events at Srebrenica were genocide; Mladić was sentenced to life imprisonment, and Radovan Karadžić's sentence was raised to life on appeal in 2019. [[c-pcw-tribunals]] In the case Bosnia and Herzegovina brought against Serbia, the ICJ ruled in 2007 that Serbia had not itself committed genocide but had violated its obligation to prevent it, and had failed to hand Mladić over to the tribunal. [[c-pcw-icj2007]]

In Rwanda the genocide against the Tutsi began on 7 April 1994 and lasted about 100 days, to mid-July; Hutu and others who opposed it were also killed. [[c-pcw-rwanda]] The number of dead is disputed. Human Rights Watch put the dead at more than half a million, three quarters of Rwanda's Tutsi; a Rwandan government census of 2000 listed 1,074,017 victims, 1,006,354 of them Tutsi; and the scholar Luc Reydams puts the maximum number of Tutsi victims at between 489,000 and 564,000. The census's Tutsi victims alone are about twice Reydams's maximum, so the gap comes mainly from method and definition: a list of victims compiled by the government against a demographic estimate of how many Tutsi lived in Rwanda and survived. [[c-pcw-rwanda-toll]]

NATO grew from 16 members to 32. Czechia, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999, seven more states in 2004 and five more between 2009 and 2023, Finland the last of them; Sweden became the 32nd member on 7 March 2024. [[c-pcw-nato]] On 1 May 2004 the European Union admitted ten states, eight of them from Central and Eastern Europe, an enlargement it describes as 'finally ending the division of Europe after the Second World War'. [[c-pcw-eu]] Whether NATO's growth turned Russia hostile is disputed. In Foreign Affairs in 2014 John Mearsheimer argued that 'the United States and its European allies share most of the responsibility for the crisis' in Ukraine and that 'the taproot of the trouble is NATO enlargement'. [[c-pcw-mearsheimer]] Michael McFaul replied that Russian policy 'changed as a result of Russian internal political dynamics', and Stephen Sestanovich that 'today's aggressive Russian policy was in place long before the mistaken Western policies'. [[c-pcw-critics]] Governments take the same sides: in 2007 Vladimir Putin called NATO expansion 'a serious provocation that reduces the level of mutual trust', while NATO says that its 'enlargement is not directed against Russia'. [[c-pcw-govts]] The war in Ukraine is taken up in 16.5.

pages.title: Globalization and China's rise
pages.lede: The World Trade Organization was founded in 1995 and China joined it in 2001. The World Bank estimates that about 1.5 billion people escaped extreme poverty between 1990 and 2022, while economists still argue over who gained and who lost from global trade.
body: The World Trade Organization was established on 1 January 1995, after the Uruguay Round of trade talks, and replaced the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) as the main framework for world trade. [[c-glob2-wto]] China, whose reforms are followed in 15.10, became its 143rd member on 11 December 2001. [[c-glob2-china-wto]] The economists David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson studied what Chinese import competition did to the United States. Alongside 'the heralded consumer benefits of expanded trade', they found 'substantial adjustment costs and distributional consequences': in exposed local labor markets unemployment stayed high 'for at least a full decade', and nationally 'offsetting employment gains in other industries have yet to materialize'. [[c-glob2-chinashock]]

Since June 2025 the World Bank has drawn its line of extreme poverty at $3.00 a day in 2021 prices, the median of the national poverty lines of 23 low-income countries. On that line the Bank estimated in June 2025 that about 838 million people lived in extreme poverty in 2022 (its live database, opened on 3 November 2026, gives about 870 million), and that some 1.5 billion people escaped it between 1990 and 2022. [[c-glob2-poverty]] [[c-glob2-pip]] Our World in Data gives 817 million for 2024 and says that over a generation the share fell 'from one in every two or three people to one in ten'. [[c-glob2-owid]] The new line raised the Bank's rate for Sub-Saharan Africa in 2022 from 37.0 to 45.5 percent. [[c-glob2-africa]] These figures move with the line and the prices behind it (16.0). [[c-now-revision]]

Who gained most? Christoph Lakner and Branko Milanovic's 'elephant curve' traced income growth from 1988 to 2008. The 'winners' were groups that in 1988 stood around the middle of the world's income distribution, 90 percent of them in Asia; the 'losers' were those around the 85th percentile, almost 90 percent of them in mature economies. [[c-glob2-elephant]] Adam Corlett objected that population grew faster in poorer countries, that the lists of countries for 1988 and 2008 differ, and that the weak growth in mature economies 'is actually driven by Japan and ex-Soviet satellite / Baltic states'. [[c-glob2-corlett]] Lakner and Milanovic replied that a second curve in their paper, the 'non-anonymous growth incidence curve', already 'addresses Corlett's compositional and demographic points'. [[c-glob2-rebuttal]]

China's National Bureau of Statistics reported growth of 5 percent in 2025, to 140.19 trillion yuan, about $20 trillion. [[c-glob2-gdp]] It also reported that the population fell for the fourth year running, by 3.39 million to 1.405 billion, with 7.92 million births. [[c-glob2-pop]] In October 2026 the IMF cut its forecast for China's growth in 2026 to 4.5 percent and projected 4 percent for 2027, citing higher energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict, weak domestic demand and a prolonged property crisis, while exports and high-tech sectors such as AI and electric vehicles grew strongly. [[c-glob2-imf]]
