pages.title: 9/11 and the wars that followed
pages.lede: On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda's attacks killed 2,977 people, and the United States went to war in Afghanistan and, in 2003, in Iraq. Estimates of the Iraqi dead differ several-fold, because they count different things and because their methods differ. After the Arab uprisings of 2011 came a decade of war in Syria, the rise and fall of the Islamic State's 'caliphate' and, in December 2024, the fall of Bashar al-Assad.
body: On 11 September 2001 nineteen al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four commercial airplanes; the attacks killed 2,977 people from 90 nations. [[c-war-911]] The US air campaign in Afghanistan began on 7 October, after the Taliban refused to hand over al-Qaeda's leaders. [[c-war-afghan]] In February 2020 the United States agreed with the Taliban to withdraw its troops, and on 15 August 2021 Taliban fighters entered Kabul as President Ghani fled. [[c-war-kabul]] US-led forces invaded Iraq on 20 March 2003 and Baghdad fell on 9 April. The war was justified by Iraq's alleged possession and manufacture of weapons of mass destruction, a claim Britannica says 'was later proved erroneous'. [[c-war-iraq]]

The Iraq Survey Group reported in 2004, and its head Charles Duelfer testified, that the weapons 'stocks do not exist', though Saddam Hussein intended to restart chemical weapons work once sanctions were lifted. [[c-war-duelfer]] Whether American officials misled the public is disputed. In June 2008 the Senate Intelligence Committee adopted its final reports by 10 votes to 5, two Republicans joining the majority, and its chairman, Jay Rockefeller, said that 'the Administration made significant claims that were not supported by the intelligence'. The Associated Press reported that the same report found the intelligence 'supported most of the administration's statements about Iraq', though officials often left out dissent and uncertainty; the committee's ranking Republican, Kit Bond, said: 'It is ironic that the Democrats would knowingly distort and misrepresent the committee's findings.' [[c-war-ssci]]

Estimates of Iraqi deaths after the invasion run from about 151,000 to about 655,000, partly because they measure different things over different periods and partly because their methods give different results. Iraq Body Count, working mainly from press and media reports, documents 200,065 to 226,628 civilian deaths from violence. [[c-now-press]] [[c-war-ibc]] The Iraq Family Health Survey of the Iraqi government and the WHO, a household survey, estimated 151,000 violent deaths from March 2003 to June 2006, within a range of 104,000 to 223,000; the WHO said this was 'about four times lower than a smaller-scale household survey conducted earlier in 2006'. [[c-war-ifhs]] That survey, by Johns Hopkins and published in The Lancet, estimated 654,965 excess deaths from all causes (range 392,979 to 942,636) in March 2003 to July 2006. [[c-war-lancet]] A later survey in PLOS Medicine estimated about 405,000 excess deaths from 2003 to 2011, with an uncertainty interval of 48,000 to 751,000. [[c-war-plos]] Across Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen and Pakistan, Brown University's Costs of War project estimates over 940,000 deaths from direct war violence in 2001-2023, more than 432,000 of them civilians. [[c-war-cow]]

A wave of pro-democracy protests and uprisings began in the Middle East and North Africa in 2010 and 2011, and in January and February 2011 protests toppled the regimes of Tunisia and Egypt. [[c-war-arabspring]] In Syria the UN human rights office estimated that 306,887 civilians were killed in the war between March 2011 and March 2021, 1.5 percent of the population. [[c-war-syria-toll]] ISIS took Mosul and declared a caliphate in June 2014, and lost Mosul and Raqqa in 2017; [[c-war-isis]] in March 2019 the Syrian Democratic Forces declared the caliphate eliminated at Baghuz. [[c-war-baghuz]] On 8 December 2024 rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham took Damascus and Assad fled, ending more than five decades of his family's rule. [[c-war-assad]] In March 2025 attacks on security forces were followed by mass killings of Alawites in the coastal region. A government committee identified 1,426 dead, most of them civilians, and said 238 members of the army and security forces had been killed in the attacks; it also said commanders 'did not give orders to commit violations'; a Reuters investigation had identified 1,479 Alawites killed; and the Supreme Alawite Council rejected the committee's findings and called for a UN-supervised inquiry. [[c-war-alawite]] In January 2026, after government forces retook parts of northern and eastern Syria, the Kurdish-led SDF agreed to a ceasefire and to integrate into the state; [[c-war-sdf]] on 25 August its commander, Mazloum Abdi, announced that it had completed its merger with the Syrian army and was dissolved. [[c-war-sdf2]] As of October 2026 the UN reported 5.5 million Syrians still displaced, Israeli forces holding expanded territory in the south, and sectarian tension in Sweida, [[c-war-syria-now]] and ISIL still a threat. [[c-war-scr]]

pages.title: The financial crisis and its aftermath
pages.lede: A US commission judged the financial crisis of 2008 avoidable, but economists still disagree about its causes. In the euro area Greece was offered a €110 billion package in 2010, and Spain, after a housing bubble, saw unemployment reach 26.2 percent in 2013. Scholars also disagree whether the populism that followed, including the Brexit vote of 2016, grew from economic shocks or from a cultural backlash.
body: In the crisis of 2008 millions of Americans lost their jobs, their savings and their homes. The US Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission concluded in 2011 that 'this crisis was avoidable', and blamed 'widespread failures in financial regulation' and 'excessive borrowing and risk-taking by households and Wall Street'. Two dissents were filed. Keith Hennessey, Douglas Holtz-Eakin and Bill Thomas traced the crisis to 'a credit bubble in the United States and Europe' and faulted the majority for ignoring its global nature; Peter J. Wallison held that 'the sine qua non of the financial crisis was U.S. government housing policy'. [[c-fin-fcic]] The majority judged that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac contributed to the crisis but were not a primary cause, and that the Community Reinvestment Act was not a significant factor. [[c-fin-gse]] The economists Atif Mian and Amir Sufi put households at the centre: in their account, 'a large run-up in household debt followed by a significantly large drop in household spending' drove the Great Recession. [[c-fin-miansufi]]

On 2 May 2010 the euro-area states and the IMF announced a three-year package of €110 billion for Greece, €80 billion from euro-area countries and €30 billion from the IMF. In return Greece was to raise value-added tax and cut its budget deficit from 13.6 percent of GDP in 2009 to below 3 percent by 2014. [[c-fin-greece]] In Spain easy bank loans had fed a housing bubble, in which house prices nearly tripled between 1997 and 2008. [[c-fin-spain-bubble]] Spain asked for a programme for its banks in June 2012; of a possible €100 billion it used about €41 billion, and it left the programme in December 2013. [[c-fin-spain-banks]] Unemployment peaked in 2013 at an annual average of 26.2 percent, some six million people; in the first quarter of that year the rate reached 27.16 percent, and 57 percent among the young. [[c-fin-spain-unemp]]

The cost of austerity is also debated. In January 2013 two IMF economists, Olivier Blanchard and Daniel Leigh, found that stronger planned budget tightening had gone with lower growth than forecast, especially early in the crisis, and read this as a sign that forecasters had underestimated its cost, though the effect looked weaker in later years. [[c-fin-multipliers]] The European Stability Mechanism, which ran Spain's bank programme, judges for its part that the reforms Spain undertook 'helped spark a surge in economic growth' after it left. [[c-fin-esm]]

On 23 June 2016 the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union by 51.9 to 48.1 percent, on a turnout of 72.2 percent. Scotland and Northern Ireland voted to remain, and David Cameron resigned as prime minister. [[c-fin-brexit]] Why such votes happened is debated. Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart explain authoritarian populism, as in Brexit and Donald Trump in the United States, by polarization over a cultural cleavage between social liberals and social conservatives. [[c-fin-norris]] Dani Rodrik finds 'compelling evidence' that globalization shocks, 'often working through culture and identity', raised support for populist movements, especially on the right. [[c-fin-rodrik]] For globalization and China's rise, see (16.2).

pages.title: Russia, Ukraine and the great powers
pages.lede: Russia fought Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The war is ongoing: as of early November 2026 there was no general ceasefire, and estimates of military casualties, for which neither government gives timely data, run well over a million. In October 2025 the United States and China agreed a one-year trade truce, extended in September 2026 to January 2027.
body: For the end of the Soviet Union see (15.14), and for the debate over NATO's enlargement (16.1). In August 2008 Georgia and Russia fought a five-day war. An inquiry commissioned by the European Union and led by the Swiss diplomat Heidi Tagliavini found that Georgia triggered it by attacking Tskhinvali, but that 'much of the Russian military action went far beyond the reasonable limits of defense'. Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili said Georgia was responding to a Russian invasion; the report found no evidence of this. Russia recognises South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent states. [[c-rus-georgia]]

On 27 March 2014 the UN General Assembly declared the referendum held in Crimea invalid, by 100 votes to 11 with 58 abstentions; many states said they would recognise neither the referendum nor Russia's annexation of Crimea that followed. [[c-rus-crimea]] On 24 February 2022 Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. On 2 March the General Assembly demanded that Russia withdraw immediately, by 141 votes to 5, with 35 abstentions, among them China and India. [[c-rus-invasion]]

Every count of the dead is incomplete. As of January 2026 the UN monitoring mission in Ukraine had verified almost 15,000 civilian deaths, at least 2,514 of them in 2025, and it says the true toll is likely considerably higher. [[c-rus-civilians]] Neither Moscow nor Kyiv gives timely data on military losses. In January 2026 CSIS estimated that from February 2022 to December 2025 Russia had suffered about 1.2 million casualties, including up to 325,000 dead, and Ukraine 500,000 to 600,000, including up to 140,000 dead; the Kremlin said the study was not 'reliable information'. [[c-rus-military]]

As of 2 November 2026 there was no general ceasefire. A local truce around Russian-occupied Oleshky, in the Kherson region, announced by the White House on 23 October to allow humanitarian aid and the evacuation of civilians, began on 27 October and ended on 1 November, and the Kremlin has repeatedly rejected calls for a wider ceasefire. [[c-rus-oleshky]] US-mediated talks, last held in February 2026, were due to resume: on 3 November the Kremlin confirmed a trilateral round in Abu Dhabi on 10-11 November. Putin wants talks on a final settlement rather than a 'short' truce; Kyiv says it is ready to resume direct talks mediated by Washington, and Zelensky wants them 'as soon as possible'. [[c-rus-talks]] Between the United States and China, Trump and Xi met at Busan on 30 October 2025 and agreed arrangements for one year: the US cut its tariff rate on Chinese goods from 57 to 47 percent, and China delayed export restrictions on five rare earth metals. [[c-rus-uschina]] In February 2026 the US Supreme Court ruled that the law used for the fentanyl-related tariffs did not authorise tariffs. Trump visited Beijing in May 2026, and when Xi came to Washington on 23 September the two sides agreed to extend the Busan arrangements from 10 November 2026 to 10 January 2027. [[c-rus-uschina2]]

pages.title: Israel and the Palestinians since 1991
pages.lede: The Oslo accords of 1993 brought mutual recognition between Israel and the PLO, but negotiations broke down in late 2000. After the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023 killed nearly 1,200 people in Israel, the war in Gaza killed tens of thousands; how many, and who they were, is counted in different ways. A ceasefire took effect in October 2025, but a year later its second phase had stalled.
body: On 13 September 1993 Israel and the PLO signed the Oslo accords in Washington. The PLO recognised the existence of the State of Israel, Israel recognised the PLO as the legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, and a permanent settlement was to be negotiated within a five-year interim period. [[c-ip-oslo]] Yitzhak Rabin shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize with Shimon Peres and Yasser Arafat; on 4 November 1995, at the end of a peace rally in Tel Aviv, a Jewish extremist assassinated him. [[c-ip-rabin]] For 1948 see (15.8).

Negotiations broke down in late 2000 and the second, or al-Aqsa, intifada followed. Israel completed its pullout from Gaza in September 2005; Hamas won the Palestinian parliamentary elections of 2006 and took control of the Gaza Strip in June 2007, after which Israel imposed sanctions. [[c-ip-intifada]] On 7 October 2023 Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing nearly 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and taking 251 hostages. [[c-ip-oct7]] In January 2024, in a case brought by South Africa, the International Court of Justice found some of the rights South Africa claimed under the Genocide Convention plausible and ordered Israel, by 15 votes to 2, to prevent acts covered by the Convention and, by 16 votes to 1, to enable humanitarian aid. It did not order a ceasefire, and it did not decide whether genocide had occurred; Israel called the accusation 'wholly unfounded'. [[c-ip-icj]] In May 2024 the court ordered Israel to halt its military offensive in Rafah in so far as it might inflict on Gaza's Palestinians conditions of life that could destroy them; Israel said it had not carried out and would not carry out such operations. The case itself continues: South Africa's presidency says Israel contested the court's jurisdiction in its Counter-Memorial of March 2026, and the court has set further written pleadings to run until May 2029. [[c-ip-icj-later]]

The dead in Gaza are counted in different ways. As of 11 October 2026 Gaza's Health Ministry reported 74,377 killed since the war began, 1,488 of them since the ceasefire; its toll does not distinguish combatants from civilians. AP reports that the ministry's records are viewed as generally reliable by the international community; Israel has questioned them, citing Hamas's control of the ministry, and the IDF says it has killed over 24,000 combatants. [[c-ip-toll]] A peer-reviewed household survey published in February 2026 estimated 75,200 violent deaths in the war's first 15 months, when the ministry had reported about 49,000. [[c-ip-lancet]] In January 2026 a senior Israeli military official, speaking anonymously, put the toll at about 71,000, but the IDF said this did 'not reflect official IDF data'. [[c-ip-idf71]]

On 21 September 2025 the UK, Australia and Canada recognised a Palestinian state; Keir Starmer said they joined over 150 countries that do so. Mahmoud Abbas welcomed this as 'an important and necessary step toward achieving a just peace'; Benjamin Netanyahu said a Palestinian state 'will not happen', and Donald Trump disapproved. [[c-ip-recognition]] A ceasefire under Trump's 20-point plan took effect on 10 or 11 October 2025; Hamas freed the last living hostages, and Israel released nearly 2,000 Palestinian prisoners and detainees. [[c-ip-ceasefire]] A year after the ceasefire its second phase had stalled. At the end of July 2026 Hamas said it had agreed to a phased plan, announced by Trump and the Board of Peace, under which it would disarm and Israel would halt its strikes and withdraw; Hamas said it would take no step unless Israel met its obligations, and tied giving up heavy weapons to Palestinian statehood, while an Israeli official said there would be no withdrawal before Hamas disarmed. As of 10 October 2026 disarmament had not begun, Israeli forces controlled, by official accounts, about 70 percent of Gaza, up from about 53 percent under the ceasefire's initial terms, and, according to Hürriyet Daily News, most of Gaza's people remained displaced. [[c-ip-phase2]] The conflict is ongoing.

pages.title: Latin America and Spain since 1990
pages.lede: Argentina defaulted in 2001; since December 2023 it has been governed by Javier Milei, whose reforms slowed inflation while growth faltered. Millions of Venezuelans have emigrated, and in January 2026 US forces seized Venezuela's leader, Nicolás Maduro. In Spain ETA dissolved in 2018, and an amnesty for those involved in the Catalan independence push, including the 2017 referendum, was found compatible with EU law by the EU Court of Justice in 2026.
body: In December 2001 Argentina defaulted on its sovereign debt and soon abandoned the regime that had pegged the peso at parity with the US dollar since 1991; the crisis had 'a devastating economic and social impact'. In 2004 the IMF's own Independent Evaluation Office concluded that 'the IMF erred by supporting inadequate policies too long'. [[c-latsp-argentina]] Javier Milei, in office since December 2023, slowed inflation by two-thirds while growth, consumption and manufacturing faltered, and cut tens of thousands of public sector jobs. His party won 40.84 percent in the midterm elections of 26 October 2025, and the US pledged a $40 billion aid package; critics blame his reforms for pushing millions deeper into poverty in their early phase. [[c-latsp-milei]] For Latin America and Iberia before 1990, see (15.12).

As of November 2024 at least 7.9 million Venezuelans had left their country, according to the R4V platform coordinated by the IOM and UNHCR; because the count rests on host governments' records, the real figure is higher. [[c-latsp-venezuela]] On 3 January 2026 US forces seized Maduro and his wife and flew them to New York to face an indictment accusing them of a narco-terrorism conspiracy. Trump said the United States would 'run the country' until a transition; legal experts questioned whether the operation was lawful, and Maduro's government called it an 'imperialist attack'. [[c-latsp-maduro]] As of 29 October 2026 Delcy Rodríguez was acting president. At the UN in September, and again on 29 October, she promised elections, the second time to be organised by a renewed electoral authority, but set no date. The opposition led by María Corina Machado, who returned from almost a year in exile on 25 October, and Edmundo González Urrutia demands a presidential election in 2027, and critics say Washington has favoured oil and investment deals with the interim government over the opposition. The transition is ongoing. [[c-latsp-rodriguez]]

In Mexico, the statistics institute INEGI reports that the homicide rate fell from 25.6 per 100,000 people in 2024 to 21.4 in 2025, below its peak of 29 in 2018-2020; the government's own figures, drawn from prosecutors' files, differ. [[c-latsp-mexico]] In Brazil, on 11 September 2025 a five-justice panel of the Supreme Court voted 4 to 1 to convict the former president Jair Bolsonaro of plotting a military coup to overturn the 2022 election, and sentenced him to more than 27 years in prison. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing, and the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, called the case a 'witch hunt'. [[c-latsp-bolsonaro]]

In Spain, ETA, created under Franco to seek an independent Basque country, killed 853 people; it declared a 'definitive end' to its terrorism in October 2011 and announced its dissolution on 2 May 2018. [[c-latsp-eta]] On 1 October 2017 Catalonia held an independence referendum that the Spanish government had declared illegal; the Catalan government reported 90.9 percent for independence on a turnout of 42.3 percent. The Catalan parliament declared independence on 27 October, Mariano Rajoy dismissed Carles Puigdemont's government and called snap elections, and Puigdemont left for Belgium. [[c-latsp-catalonia]] After the inconclusive 2023 elections Pedro Sánchez proposed an amnesty in exchange for the Catalan secessionists' support in parliament; conservatives opposed it, and on 16 July 2026 the EU Court of Justice ruled that 'EU law does not preclude the Spanish amnesty law'. [[c-latsp-amnesty]]

pages.title: India, Africa and the world's population
pages.lede: In 1991 India began to open its economy; on UN projections it passed China as the most populous country in 2023, and the World Bank calls it the fastest-growing major economy, though how its growth is measured is disputed. The world reached 8 billion people in 2022, and the UN projects a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s, as fertility falls and sub-Saharan Africa's population grows by about two-thirds by 2050.
body: In 1991, faced with a huge balance-of-payments deficit, India's finance minister, Manmohan Singh, began reforms that opened up the economy, moving it, in the AP's words, away from 'a socialist-patterned economy' and toward 'a capitalist model'. [[c-pop-1991]] (On China's reforms from 1978, see 15.10; on globalization, 16.2.) As of November 2025 the World Bank called India the fastest-growing major economy, with growth of 6.5 percent in 2024-25, [[c-pop-growth]] and on 27 February 2026 a new official GDP series, based on 2022-23 rather than 2011-12, was released; its provisional estimate of June 2026 put growth in 2025-26 at 7.7 percent. [[c-pop-newseries]] Measured at the World Bank's line of $2.15 a day, extreme poverty fell from 16.2 percent of Indians in 2011-12 to 2.3 percent in 2022-23, lifting 171 million people above the line; at the newer $3.00 line it fell from 27.1 to 5.3 percent. [[c-pop-poverty]]

How far to trust India's growth figures is disputed. In 2019 Arvind Subramanian, the government's former chief economic adviser, estimated that growth between 2011-12 and 2016-17 had been about 4.5 percent a year, not the official 7 percent. The Prime Minister's Economic Advisory Council, in a reply by Bibek Debroy, Rathin Roy, Surjit Bhalla, Charan Singh and Arvind Virmani, rejected his method and his 'blind trust in a private agency'. [[c-pop-gdpdebate]] In November 2025 the IMF graded India's national accounts 'C', meaning that their shortcomings 'somewhat hamper surveillance', and cited the old base year among other problems. Indian officials, among them Urjit Patel, India's executive director at the IMF, answered that IMF staff themselves had found the statistics 'broadly adequate for surveillance'. [[c-pop-imf]]

The UN marked 15 November 2022 as the day the world's population reached 8 billion, [[c-pop-8bn]] and projected that India would pass China as the most populous country in April 2023. [[c-pop-india-china]] Its World Population Prospects 2024 projects growth from 8.2 billion in 2024 to about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s, then a slight fall to about 10.2 billion by 2100. [[c-pop-peak]] Between 1990 and 2024 world fertility fell from 3.31 children per woman to 2.25, while life expectancy at birth rose from 64.0 to 73.3 years. [[c-pop-fertility]] Population has already peaked in 63 countries and areas, among them China, Germany, Japan and Russia, [[c-pop-peaked]] and by the late 2070s people aged 65 and over are projected to outnumber children under 18. [[c-pop-ageing]]

Sub-Saharan Africa's population is projected to rise by about two-thirds by 2050. In nine countries, among them Angola, the Central African Republic, DR Congo, Niger and Somalia, it is projected to double between 2024 and 2054, and Nigeria, India, Pakistan and the United States are among 126 countries expected to keep growing through 2054. China's population, by contrast, is projected to fall by about 200 million, close to 14 percent, between 2024 and 2054. [[c-pop-africa]] People also move. The UN counts 304 million international migrants in 2024, 3.7 percent of the world's population and nearly twice the 154 million of 1990, [[c-pop-migrants]] and the World Bank expected migrants' recorded remittances to low- and middle-income countries to reach $685 billion in 2024, with India the largest recipient at about $129 billion. [[c-pop-remit]]

pages.title: Religion in the 21st century
pages.lede: Between 2010 and 2020, Pew finds, the number of Christians grew but their share of the world fell, mainly because of disaffiliation from religion, while Muslims grew by more than all other religions combined. Christianity's weight has shifted to sub-Saharan Africa. In 2013 a pope resigned for the first time since 1415, and his successors were the first Latin American and the first American popes.
body: In the Pew Research Center's count for 2010-2020, the number of Christians rose by 122 million, to 2.3 billion, but their share of the world's population fell 1.8 points, to 28.8 percent. [[c-relig-christians]] Muslims grew by 347 million, more than all other religions combined, to 25.6 percent, which Pew attributes largely to their 'relatively young age structure and high fertility rate'. [[c-relig-muslims]] The religiously unaffiliated grew by 270 million, to 1.9 billion, or 24.2 percent, and Pew calls 'religious disaffiliation' the main driver of the fall in the Christian share. [[c-relig-nones]] Hindus held steady at 14.9 percent, while Buddhists were the only major group to shrink in number. [[c-relig-others]]

Christianity's centre of gravity has moved south: as of 2020, 30.7 percent of the world's Christians lived in sub-Saharan Africa and 22.3 percent in Europe. [[c-relig-south]] Pew's projections of 2015 expected four in ten Christians to live there by 2050, and near parity between Muslims and Christians by then; [[c-relig-proj2015]] the same projections expected the unaffiliated share to fall, from 16 percent in 2010 to 13 percent by 2050, but Pew's later count, on a different baseline, shows it rising between 2010 and 2020. [[c-relig-nones]] Pew also counted about 279 million pentecostal and 305 million charismatic Christians in 2010, though such counts vary with definitions. [[c-relig-pente]]

Counts of the Jewish people depend on definitions. Pew gives 14.8 million for 2020. Sergio DellaPergola estimated a 'core' population of 15,736,800 on 1 January 2024, 7,153,000 of them in Israel and 6.3 million in the United States; counting more widely, his 'enlarged' figure is about 21.8 million, and about 24.7 million people, Jewish and non-Jewish, are eligible to immigrate to Israel under its Law of Return. [[c-relig-jews]] In September 2025 Israel's statistics bureau estimated 10,148,000 people in the country, about 7.76 million of them 'Jews and others'. [[c-relig-israelpop]] (On Israel and the Palestinians, see 16.6.)

In the Catholic Church, Benedict XVI resigned as from 28 February 2013, the first pope to do so since 1415. [[c-relig-benedict]] His successor, Francis, the first Latin American pope, died on Easter Monday, 21 April 2025, aged 88. [[c-relig-francis]] On 8 May 2025 the cardinals elected Robert Prevost, an Augustinian who had served as a missionary in Peru, later led the church in Chiclayo and then headed the Vatican office that vets bishops, as Leo XIV, the first American pope. [[c-relig-leo]] (On Nostra Aetate, see 15.14.) Views of religion in politics vary widely: across 35 countries a median of 30 percent say it is very important that their leader stand up for people with their religious beliefs, from around seven in ten in Bangladesh and Indonesia to 5 percent in Japan. [[c-relig-leaders]]

pages.title: Climate and the planet
pages.lede: The IPCC concludes that human activities have 'unequivocally' caused global warming. 2024 was the warmest year on record, and 2023-2025 was the first three-year period to average more than 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, the more ambitious goal set at Paris in 2015. Emissions reached a record in 2025, and how fast to cut them, and at what cost, is argued over by economists and governments.
body: The IPCC's Synthesis Report of 2023 states: 'Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming'. Warming had reached 1.1°C above 1850-1900 in 2011-2020. [[c-clim-ipcc]] It judged it 'more likely than not' that warming would reach 1.5°C in the near term (2021-2040), even under its very low-emission scenario. [[c-clim-near15]] The World Meteorological Organization confirmed 2024 as the warmest year on record, at about 1.55°C above the pre-industrial level, but stressed that this alone 'does NOT mean' the Paris long-term goals have failed, since they refer to long-term warming. [[c-clim-2024]] Copernicus ranked 2025 third-warmest, at 1.47°C, found that 2023-2025 was the first three-year period to average above 1.5°C, and warned that the long-term limit could be reached by the end of this decade. [[c-clim-2025]] (On how data series shape our view of recent history, see 16.0.)

The Paris Agreement, adopted on 12 December 2015, aims to hold warming 'well below 2°C' and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C; as of 27 January 2026 it had 194 Parties. [[c-clim-paris]] That was the day the United States' withdrawal took effect, making it the only country to have quit the pact twice. [[c-clim-us]] At COP30 in Belém in November 2025, rich nations agreed to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035, but a 'roadmap' away from fossil fuels, backed by the EU and others, was dropped. [[c-clim-cop30deal]] France's minister Monique Barbut blamed Saudi Arabia, Russia, India and others. Saudi Arabia's deputy environment minister, Osama Faqeeha, said that 'the issue is the emissions, it's not the fuel', and India said it did not oppose a plan, but that countries must not be 'called to adhere to a uniform pathway'. [[c-clim-cop30views]]

Emissions are still rising. The Global Carbon Project projected a record 38.1 billion tonnes of fossil CO2 in 2025, against a remaining budget of about 170 billion tonnes for 1.5°C. [[c-clim-gcp]] Counting all greenhouse gases, the EU's EDGAR database finds a record 54 billion tonnes in 2025: China emitted 29.5 percent, the United States 11.1 percent and India 8.3 percent, and the US had the largest absolute rise. [[c-clim-edgar]] History reverses the ranking. From 1850 to 2021 the United States emitted 20.3 percent of all CO2 and China 11.4 percent, and cumulative emissions, in the words of the Union of Concerned Scientists, are 'the dominant driver of climate change'. [[c-clim-cumul]]

The IPCC's pathways for 1.5°C cut greenhouse-gas emissions by a median of 43 percent by 2030 and 60 percent by 2035, compared with 2019. [[c-clim-paths]] Solar power has become cheap: IRENA puts the cost of electricity from new solar plants commissioned in 2024 at US$0.043 per kWh, on average 41 percent below the cheapest fossil-fuel alternatives. [[c-clim-solar]] Estimates of the costs and benefits of going faster differ widely. Nicholas Stern's review of 2006 found that unchecked warming would cost the equivalent of 'at least 5 percent of global GDP each year now and forever', against around 1 percent a year for action. Bjørn Lomborg writes of net-zero promises: 'Every dollar in cost delivers perhaps 16 cents of climate benefits.' [[c-clim-cost]]

pages.title: Technology and health
pages.lede: By 2025 almost three-quarters of humanity used the internet, and whether smartphones and social media harmed the young had become a public argument. COVID-19 killed more than 7 million people by official count and, on WHO's latest estimate, about 22.1 million in excess deaths in 2020-2023, while mRNA vaccines were approved within a year of the first report from Wuhan. Since November 2022 ChatGPT, a large language model, has reached 900 million weekly users by its maker's count (February 2026).
body: About 6 billion people, almost three-quarters of the world's population, used the internet in 2025, according to the ITU, while 2.2 billion remained offline, most of them in low- and middle-income countries. [[c-tech-internet]] What smartphones and social media have done to the young is disputed. The core idea of Jonathan Haidt's The Anxious Generation (2024), in Fortune's summary, is that 'something changed in the lives of American young people somewhere around 2010 to 2015', and Zach Rausch, Haidt's chief researcher, says much of what the book has focused on is 'irrefutable'. Candice Odgers of the University of California, Irvine, wrote in Nature that Haidt is 'telling stories that are unsupported by research', and Andrew Przybylski of Oxford said: 'Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.' [[c-tech-haidt]] Australia has acted all the same: its ban on social media accounts for under-16s took effect on 10 December 2025, with fines of up to A$49.5 million. [[c-tech-ban]] By mid-January 2026 platforms had revoked about 4.7 million accounts; Meta, privacy advocates and some teenagers' groups criticised the law, and the eSafety Commissioner said there were no long-term trends yet. [[c-tech-bandebate]]

On 31 December 2019 WHO's office in China picked up a statement from Wuhan's health commission on cases of 'viral pneumonia'. WHO declared an international emergency on 30 January 2020 and called COVID-19 a pandemic on 11 March. [[c-tech-wuhan]] By December 2024 more than 7 million deaths had been reported to WHO, which says the true numbers are likely higher. [[c-tech-reported]] WHO's estimate of excess deaths, the deaths above those that would have been expected, is about 14.9 million for 2020 and 2021 alone, 81 percent of them in middle-income countries. [[c-tech-excess]] In World Health Statistics 2026 WHO estimated about 22.1 million excess deaths for 2020 to 2023, against 7.0 million reported COVID-19 deaths; excess deaths peaked in 2021, at 10.4 million. [[c-tech-excess2]] Vaccines came fast: two mRNA vaccines, with protective effects of around 95 percent, were approved as early as December 2020, and Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman won the 2023 Nobel Prize for the discoveries that made them possible. [[c-tech-mrna]]

Today's machine learning rests on artificial neural networks: John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton won the 2024 Nobel Prize in physics for 'foundational discoveries and inventions' that enable it. [[c-tech-nobel24]] In June 2017 Google researchers proposed the Transformer, an architecture based 'solely on attention mechanisms'. [[c-tech-transformer]] OpenAI launched ChatGPT, a large language model based on a 'Generative Pre-training Transformer', on 30 November 2022; Britannica notes that such models can sometimes produce inaccurate information. [[c-tech-chatgpt]] By February 2026 OpenAI said 900 million people used it every week, a figure that comes from the company itself. [[c-tech-users]] Some scientists, Hinton among them, worry that AI could become superintelligent; many researchers disagree. [[c-tech-aidebate]]

All of this is recent, and its history is provisional. Timothy Garton Ash calls the history of the present 'this strange mongrel genre', written 'between journalism and scholarship'. [[c-tech-present]] That is why the figures on this page carry dates: the excess-death estimates cover set periods (2020-21, and 2020-2023), the user numbers come from the company itself, and the effects of social media are still disputed. [[c-tech-excess]] [[c-tech-excess2]] [[c-tech-users]] [[c-tech-haidt]] (On how we know recent history, see 16.0.)
